title: The view from above
hook: Marcus pictures the world from high up: herds of people, weddings, births, deaths (Meditations 9.30)

segments.voice: Yesterday: itadakimasu, one of the pauses many traditions take before eating. Your line was the food arrived.

You've probably had this happen on a plane. The wheels leave the runway, and in a minute the city you've rushed through all week turns into a map. The highway you sat in traffic on is a gray thread. The office is a speck. Somewhere down there is your kitchen, and the argument you had in it this morning. For a moment, it all looks different. Not unimportant. Just smaller, and somehow gentler. A Roman emperor practiced that feeling on purpose, with no plane, using only his imagination. This week is about seeing life at its true size, and remembering we're mortal.
screen: `THE WHEELS LEAVE THE RUNWAY.` → `THE CITY BECOMES A MAP.` → `SMALLER, AND GENTLER.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius keeps coming back to an exercise in the Meditations. In George Long's translation, one passage begins: Look down from above on the countless herds of men and their countless solemnities. Then he lists what he sees: the voyages in storm and calm, people being born, living together, dying. Elsewhere he imagines the lives of people long ago: marrying, raising children, falling ill, feasting, flattering, plotting, all of it gone now. The French historian Pierre Hadot, who spent his life studying ancient philosophy as a practice, gave this exercise its modern name: the view from above. Why would an emperor do this? Partly to shrink his worries to their true size. From high enough, the insult at court and the delayed shipment look like what they are: small. Partly to shrink his pride. From above, an emperor's palace is a speck too. But the third thing is the part people miss. The view from above isn't cold. Marcus doesn't look down and sneer. He sees everyone at once, doing the same human things: being born, marrying, working, grieving. From up there you can't tell the emperor from the baker. It's hard to stay furious at one small figure when you can see how small and how human they all are, you included. So today's line has two halves. So small: the worry, the ego, the argument. So loved: the people, each one living a whole life down there.
screen: `LOOK DOWN FROM ABOVE.` · `WORRIES AT THEIR TRUE SIZE.` · `THE EMPEROR IS A SPECK TOO.` · `EVERYONE, DOING HUMAN THINGS.` · then, large: `SO SMALL, SO LOVED.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself where you're sitting, then rise slowly through the ceiling: your roof, your street, a neighbor walking a dog, then the whole town like a map, a mile below. Somewhere down there is today's worry; notice its size, and all the lives around it. Then, slowly, come back down.
Hadot. The historian who named Marcus's exercise of picturing the world from high up, so worries shrink and people come into view. Today's word.
Your line: so small, so loved. The view from above takes you out of the traffic, so you can see the city. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often use the view from above, a guided imagining from Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, rising in the mind until their own worries and the whole human scene can be seen at once.
